newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nippon Credit Australia sees sale in 3 mths.
newsitem.headline: Nippon Credit Australia sees sale in 3 mths.

text.p: Nippon Credit Bank's (NCB) Australian unit said on Friday it had appointed Hambros Corporate Finance to advise NCB on the sale of Nippon Credit Australia within the next three months.
"We're up for sale," Nippon Credit Australia Deputy Managing Director Fraser Read-Smith told Reuters.
NCB, hit hard by non-performing real estate loans, announced on April 1 a restructuring that included the withdrawal from foreign operations like Nippon Credit Australia.
Read-Smith said Hambros had been retained to advise on the sales and had received a lot of inquiries.
"There's been quite a lot of interest from other banking and financial organisations and we're looking forward to the possibilities," Read-Smith said.
He said Nippon Credit's Singapore, Los Angeles and Zurich units had been sold off or closed down by June 30, but that Nippon Credit Australia hoped to be sold as an independent going concern.
Nippon Credit Australia had focussed on Australian structured finance and project finance infrastructure and aimed to continue in those areas.

Read-Smith said Nippon Credit Australia was ready to launch a new fund called Infrastructure 2000 fund which aimed to raise A$200 million, but wanted its ownership structure settled before proceeding.
He said Hambros was still canvassing potential purchasers and hoped to have whittled the field down to a few within two to three weeks.
Nippon Credit Australia, which started Australian operations in 1986, posted a net profit of A$9.3 million in the six months to June 30 after earning a net A$8.7 million in calendar 1996.
Nippon Credit Australia's pre-tax return on average risk weighted assets was 5.42 percent in the first half of 1997, up from 2.16 percent in the full 1996 year.
Its cost to income ratio rell to 22.1 percent from 34.1 percent in 1996.
Nippon Credit Australia had total assets as at June 30 of A$605.31 million and net assets of A$175.52 million.
But Read-Smith said there was about A$114 million worth of non-redeemable preference shares which would be repatriated to NCB before the sale, leaving net assets of about A$61 million.
Given these net assets, a bank like Nippon Credit Australia could be expected to sell for between A$50 million and A$100 million.
